_note: Every number used to measure market reactions and to draw conclusions, with the reason for it. Change a value here (and bump version) rather than in code; each assessment records this file's hash. See docs/07-coverage-and-settings.md.

rationale.estimation_days: Normal behaviour (alpha, beta, residual noise) is estimated on 120 trading days (~6 months), within the 120-250 day range common in the event-study literature (MacKinlay 1997): long enough for a stable beta, short enough to reflect the current business.
rationale.gap_days: 10 trading days between the estimation window and the event keep pre-event leakage and drift out of 'normal' behaviour.
rationale.windows.price: Day 0 and +1: most of the price response to firm-specific news happens within a day or two; +1 also catches news released late in the session.
rationale.windows.volume: Days 0 to +2: trading activity stays elevated slightly longer than prices as investors rebalance.
rationale.windows.volatility: Days 0 to +4 (one trading week): uncertainty takes longer to settle than the price level, and a variance estimate needs a few days.
rationale.significance_z: |z| >= 1.96 is a two-sided 5% test: a move this large happens on about 1 normal day in 20.
rationale.exchanges: Each company is measured on its home exchange. News published after that exchange's 16:00 close can only be traded on its next session, so the event day moves forward (New York for US listings, Sydney for ASX). Benchmarks: SPY (S&P 500 ETF) for US large caps; STW (SPDR S&P/ASX 200 ETF) for ASX companies - the market factor each stock is compared against.
rationale.ticker_suffixes: Tickers carry their exchange: 'BHP.AX' is ASX, a bare ticker is US. vendor_suffix maps this to the price vendor's codes (EODHD: .US, .AU).

rationale.confirming_origins: Three independent origins (not three copies) make a coordinated error unlikely; a filing or the company's own statement confirms on its own.
rationale.corroborating_origins: Two independent origins is the classic journalistic standard for corroboration.
rationale.high_support: 'High' needs the market to confirm a clear majority (>= 60%) of the measurable expectations.
rationale.medium_support: Below 40% the playbook's expectations are mostly not borne out, so confidence cannot be more than low.
rationale.min_events_for_calibration: Brown & Warner (1985) study event-study tests on samples of 50 events; below ~20 a single outlier dominates the average, so results from fewer events are shown as 'indicative' only. The same minimum applies before a link window is replaced by a calibrated one.
rationale.window_quantile: A storyline's link window should cover the time to the next stage in most observed cases: the 90th percentile of observed gaps between stages.
rationale.window_margin: +25% on top of that percentile, because small samples underestimate the tail and a slightly long window costs little (a few extra searches).
rationale.significance_z: Same two-sided 5% threshold as for single events, applied to the cross-sectional (BMP) statistic.
rationale.overlap_trading_days: Stages closer than the longest measurement window (volatility, day 0 to +4) share trading days, so their separate reactions cannot be told apart. Example: a leader's misconduct story and resignation within a week. The assessment then also reports one combined reaction for the whole sequence.
rationale.confirmation_days: Other outlets follow up a real company story within days. A report that no independent source has confirmed after 7 days counts against its source's track record; younger reports are not judged yet.
rationale.unconfirmed_weight: 'Not confirmed by anyone else' is weaker evidence than 'shown to be wrong' (a true scoop can stay exclusive), so it counts half as much as a confirmation. Idea from truth-discovery research: sources whose claims others corroborate are more trustworthy (Yin, Han & Yu 2008, IEEE TKDE).

rationale.near_duplicate_jaccard: Two articles sharing >= 80% of their 5-word shingles are treated as copies (syndication or light rewrites); the shingle-resemblance method is Broder (1997).
rationale.near_duplicate_days: Copies of wire stories appear within hours to a few days; comparing against 3 days of articles keeps the check cheap.
rationale.copy_novelty: Re-printed news is not new information (Tetlock 2011: investors over-react to stale news, which then reverses), so copies count at 20% of a fresh report in impact.

rationale.window_days: Every company we follow is large and covered weekly by the financial press, so a week with no article naming it means our sources or our name matching miss it (as with Apple before exact_case_aliases: 1 article in a year). Checked after every round; shown on How it works.
